title: Inflammation-driven cellular selection impacts X-linked mosaicism in the epidermis
summary: In eutherian females, the choice of which X chromosome gets embryonically inactivated is thought to be random. Somatic tissues are thus assumed to comprise cells with a 50:50 ratio of maternal:paternal X active. However, a phenomenon known as X-skewing has been observed, wherein tissue composition shifts to be dominated by cells expressing one X or the other. On a gross level, such X-skewing is phenotypically silent except in the case where one X-chromosome carries a disease mutation. Here, by leveraging a mouse model of an X-linked disease called Incontinentia Pigmenti, caused by heterozygous mutations in the NF-kB effector, Nemo, we explore how X-linked cellular dynamics shape progenitor biology in the epidermis. Lineage tracing with X-linked reporters shows that at birth, the epidermis is unexpectedly skewed toward mutant cells. Within a week, as inflammation emerges, these dynamics reverse leaving surviving animals with almost entirely wild-type epithelium. The shift is driven by loss rather than growth since mutant cells adopt an aberrant fate and die at higher rates than their wild-type neighbours; proliferation rises in both populations. Notably, wild-type proliferation scales with local tissue composition, suggesting these cells calibrate their response to the extent of the mutant burden to compensate appropriately for tissue loss. Depleting macrophages, the principal TNF- source, attenuates inflammation, mutant cell death and ultimately is expected to preserve the mutant population. Altogether, our results identify inflammation as a selective force capable of resolving deleterious mosaicism, not only in the context of an X-linked disease, but within any dynamic, clonally heterogeneous epithelium.

title: The staphylococcal type VII secretion system delays inflammatory cell death during macrophage infection
summary: The human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus is a facultatively intracellular bacterium that can replicate and survive within macrophages. While macrophage-mediated immune modulation is pivotal in S. aureus pathogenesis, bacterial manipulation of macrophage pathways remains poorly understood. The specialised type VII secretion system (T7SSb) is an important virulence-associated factor during staphylococcal infection, although, unlike its mycobacterial counterparts, its role in controlling staphylococcal-macrophage interactions remains unclear. Employing high-resolution time-lapse imaging, we demonstrated an induction of pore-induced cellular traps (PITs) during S. aureus infection of macrophages in vitro, with a higher number of PITs forming in macrophages infected with S. aureus lacking EssC ({Delta}essC), a central T7SS transporter. Interestingly, {Delta}essC-infected macrophages displayed increased bacterial escape compared to wild type (WT)-infected cells, implicating a role for T7SS in delaying macrophage cell death. Changes in cell death were accompanied by a reduction in efferocytosis of {Delta}essC-infected cells in vitro. Investigation of cell death signalling markers in WT and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages demonstrated that the T7SS delayed induction of key cell death pathways, necroptosis and pyroptosis, and a dual RNAseq analysis of WT- and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages indicated a T7SS-dependent modulation of bacterial oxidative stress and selected host chemokines. We also demonstrated that T7SS effectors, EsxA and EsxC individually delayed macrophage cell death. Interestingly, {Delta}esxC mutants demonstrated accelerated calcium fluxes, indicating that the T7SS-mediated suppression of cellular calcium signalling may cause the delay in cell death. Furthermore, in a murine skin infection model, we showed that effector and transporter mutants have distinct S. aureus infection outcomes. Our findings suggest for the first time a key role for T7SSb proteins in controlling macrophage cell death, which impacts staphylococcal survival within the host during infection.

title: Acclimation capacity of two-banded seabream juveniles (Diplodus vulgaris) to port conditions: implications for the role of ports as nursery habitats
summary: orts are highly anthropized coastal environments characterized by elevated pollution and habitat alteration, posing significant challenges for marine organisms. However, the effects of port conditions on juvenile coastal fish using ports as nurseries remain poorly understood. Here, we combined field sampling and in situ caging experiments to investigate the genetic structure (RAD-seq), physiological condition (growth, lipid content, CYP1A-dependent biotransformation activity), and transcriptomic responses (RNA-seq) of juvenile two-banded sea bream (Diplodus vulgaris) exposed to port conditions. Juveniles from a port site were compared with individuals from two nearby non-port sites (T0), before fish from all populations were caged within the port for one month (T1). The site furthest from the port was slightly genetically differentiated. Port juveniles were larger and fatter at T0 than fish from non-port populations, and all populations showed differential regulation of lipid metabolism, xenobiotic detoxification, hypoxia response, and circadian rhythm pathways between T0 and T1. After one month of caging, weight differences persisted while muscle lipid content sharply declined in all populations. Only juveniles from the site furthest from the port significantly grew between T0 and T1. Port juveniles had a different transcriptional response to caging than non-port juveniles, with a higher expression of genes associated with energy metabolism, while non-port individuals overexpressed genes in detoxification, lipid metabolism, and oncogenic pathways. While we admit limitations related to caging conditions, our results suggest that port conditions strongly influence juvenile fish physiology and transcriptional levels, potentially promoting short-term acclimation strategies that could have long-term consequences for health and survival.
